clue.text: Roderick hurried along with the Benedictine

parts.note: hurried, in the past tense, means ran
Dom is the title given to a Benedictine monk

explanation.surface: A man called Roderick rushes along in the company of a monk.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on literature: Roderick Random is the hero of Tobias Smollett's eighteenth-century novel, so his surname completes the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Smollett's picaresque hero is named Roderick Random, so the surname is what follows that first name.

clue.text: Light vehicle for the N.U.R.?

parts.note: these letters make the word run when turned about; the N.U.R. was the National Union of Railwaymen

explanation.surface: A small car offered to the railway workers' union.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as RUN ABOUT: turn RUN about and you get NUR. The N.U.R. was Britain's National Union of Railwaymen.
explanation.definitionFit: A small car for short trips is a light vehicle.

clue.text: Dishevelled bear sank in this state

indicators.note: something dishevelled is untidy, so the letters are messed up

explanation.surface: An unkempt bear sinks somewhere in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dishevelled' rearranges BEAR and SANK.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the United States, in the Great Plains, with Lincoln as its capital.

clue.text: Never too confused to be in harmony

indicators.note: confused letters are jumbled, so these two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is never too muddled to sing in tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' rearranges NEVER and TOO; 'to be' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A harmonic sounding above the fundamental note is part of musical harmony.

clue.text: Indicating it's time for the boss to use his pen?

definitions.text: Indicating it's time for the boss to use his pen?

parts.words: Indicating it's time for the boss to use his pen?
parts.note: read as two words, the boss must put his name to the day's letters before they go out, while the whole is a pointer showing the way

explanation.surface: A secretary hints that the boss should get writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as SIGN POST: the letters in the outgoing mail need the boss's signature. As one word it is a roadside pointer, the thing that is 'indicating'.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadside pointer is a device for indicating direction, and signing the outgoing mail is the boss's pen work.

clue.text: This party views matters with some concern

definitions.text: This party views matters with some concern

parts.words: This party views matters with some concern
parts.note: the party is a person in a legal sense, one with a stake who therefore cares about matters

explanation.surface: A political group looks at affairs with worry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'party' suggests politics, but here it is a person with a stake; 'concern' means involvement, not worry.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with a stake in a matter has a concern in it, as with an involved party.

clue.text: You'll get pinched if you forbid return to bed

indicators.note: return means the word for forbid is read backwards

parts.note: to ban is to forbid
taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning that banning someone from going back to bed will get you arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns BAN into NAB.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinched in the slang sense of arrested or caught means collared.

clue.text: Mum, hi! Do come up here

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the pieces are read from bottom to top

parts.note: Ma is a word for mum
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A child calls to their mother to come upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'come up' turns MA HI DO round, giving ODIHAM, a small town in Hampshire, England, home to an RAF station; 'here' points to the place.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue's place word points at a Hampshire town, a location rather than a definition in words.

clue.text: It's stretching things to the limit to make these fit

definitions.text: It's stretching things to the limit to make these fit

parts.words: It's stretching things to the limit to make these fit
parts.note: the garments named are close-fitting and elastic, stretched over the limbs

explanation.surface: Someone complains that something is being pushed too far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stretching things to the limit' sounds like exaggeration; read it literally, the garment is stretched to the limbs to fit.
explanation.definitionFit: Close-fitting hosiery covering the legs and hips is stretched on to fit snugly.

clue.text: Gold coins for the exalted

definitions.meaning: the noble was a medieval English gold coin
people of high rank, the aristocracy

explanation.surface: Gold money is set aside for people of high rank.
explanation.definitionFit: The medieval English noble was a gold coin, and aristocrats of exalted rank are peers of the realm.

clue.text: In which Charlotte had a go at a Broadway boy?

parts.note: to have a go at someone with a knife is to stab
Bing is taken as a New York showman's name, as in Bing Crosby or Rudolf Bing of the Metropolitan Opera

explanation.surface: Someone named Charlotte has a go at a young man from the New York theatre world.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlotte Corday killed the revolutionary Marat with a knife in his bath in 1793, so her deed was a knife attack; 'at a' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte Corday's assassination of Marat was carried out with a kitchen knife, a knife attack.

clue.text: Curses stimulate some furnaces

definitions.meaning: oaths or exclamations of annoyance, as in 'blast it!'
air is forced into a blast furnace to raise its heat

explanation.surface: Someone swears while stoking the furnaces.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath like 'damn' is an exclamation of anger, and forcing air into smelting furnaces drives them hotter.

clue.text: Digger's reward for a crafty bit of information, we hear

indicators.note: signals that the phrase is pronounced, giving a word that sounds like it

parts.note: a crafty, or arty, piece of information is an 'arty fact'

explanation.surface: An archaeologist is paid off with a cunning tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digger' is an archaeologist, not a gardener; 'crafty' is used in its sense of arty, to do with arts and crafts.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaeologist's excavation is rewarded by finding man-made objects of the past.

clue.text: Cantering wildly round the pole in a delightful way

indicators.note: round means the rearranged letters go around the pole letter
wildly says the letters of cantering run riot into a new order

parts.note: N is the north pole

explanation.surface: A horse canters madly around a post in charming fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wildly' rearranges CANTERING; 'round' puts it about N.
explanation.definitionFit: Something charming that holds you spellbound delights you.

clue.text: "Drink down all ——" (Merry Wives)

parts.note: a quotation with its last word missing, from Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor, where Page proposes a toast to drink away ill feeling

explanation.surface: A line from a Shakespeare comedy with a word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act 1 of The Merry Wives of Windsor, Page says 'Come, we have a hot venison pasty to dinner: come, gentlemen, I hope we shall drink down all ...'; the answer fills the blank.
explanation.definitionFit: Page's toast invites the company to wash away their ill will and hostility over a drink.

clue.text: Spoken in the dimness by a virtuous teacher

indicators.note: in places the spoken word within the word for dimness

parts.note: mist brings dimness
oral means spoken

explanation.surface: A good-living schoolmaster speaks in the gloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who lectures others on right conduct is a preacher of ethics.

clue.text: Like one of the lordly ones?

definitions.text: Like one of the lordly ones?

parts.words: Like one of the lordly ones?
parts.note: the lordly ones are lords of the manor, and the adjective describes what belongs to their estates

explanation.surface: Someone acts as if they were an aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lordly' suggests haughty behaviour; here it means those who own a manor.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes what relates to a country estate held by a lord.

clue.text: Betting among the Doves ?

parts.note: small bets, and the quick wing movements of birds

explanation.surface: Gambling going on among pigeon fanciers.
explanation.walkthrough: A small bet is a flutter in British slang; doves flutter their wings.
explanation.definitionFit: Small wagers are casual gambles, and flapping wings is the movement of birds.

clue.text: Open house for a general punch-up

definitions.meaning: an event where anyone may take part or help themselves
a brawl in which everyone joins in

explanation.surface: A party open to all turns into a brawl.
explanation.definitionFit: Something anyone may join is unrestricted, and a brawl involving everyone is a melee.

clue.text: Flesh is heir to a thousand natural ones

definitions.text: Flesh is heir to a thousand natural ones

parts.words: Flesh is heir to a thousand natural ones
parts.note: a quotation from Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' speech about the blows human beings must suffer

explanation.surface: A philosophical line about the frailty of the body.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet speaks of 'the heart-ache and the thousand natural ... that flesh is heir to'; the missing word is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's speech lists the sudden blows and upsets of life that the body inherits.

clue.text: Newman's friend is due for a change

indicators.note: for a change says these letters take on a new order

explanation.surface: A friend of Newman's is overdue for something different.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a change' rearranges DUE FOR. Richard Hurrell Froude was John Henry Newman's close friend in the Oxford Movement.
explanation.definitionFit: Hurrell Froude was a companion of Cardinal Newman in the Oxford Movement.

clue.text: The Entertainer (French edition)

parts.note: the French word for a male performer who recites, borrowed into English

explanation.surface: The French translation of a play or ragtime piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Entertainer' suggests the Osborne play or Joplin rag; the answer is the French word for a reciter.
explanation.definitionFit: A man who gives dramatic monologues or recitations is a French-named performer.

clue.text: I'm returning at one after her, might leontes have said?

indicators.note: after her places those letters behind the word her

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: returning means the letters of I'm are read backwards

parts.note: taken as written as the letters I and M
taken as written

explanation.surface: A line imagining what a character in a play might have said on coming back at one o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns I'M round to MI; MI with ONE comes 'after' HER. Leontes, King of Sicilia in Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale, might call his queen's name.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Winter's Tale the jealous King Leontes is married to Queen Hermione, whose name he might well call.

clue.text: Manager to a top trumpeter

parts.note: the trumpeter is an elephant, and its manager is the driver who sits on top of it

explanation.surface: Someone looks after the business of a leading jazz trumpet player.
explanation.walkthrough: The trumpeter is not a musician but an elephant, which trumpets; 'top' is where its handler sits, on the elephant's neck.
explanation.definitionFit: In India an elephant's keeper and driver rides on its neck and directs it.

clue.text: Composer makes a hit on arriving at the Emerald Isle

parts.note: a coup is a striking success, a hit
Erin is a poetic name for Ireland, the Emerald Isle

explanation.surface: A songwriter scores a success on reaching Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: François Couperin was a French Baroque keyboard composer.

clue.text: With an end that has a somewhat fishy beginning

definitions.text: With an end that has a somewhat fishy beginning

parts.words: With an end that has a somewhat fishy beginning
parts.note: a word meaning limited, whose first three letters spell the fishy part a fish swims with

explanation.surface: A story whose ending follows a suspicious start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With an end' is the meaning; the rest says the word starts with FIN, a fish's swimming limb.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bounded or limited has an end, rather than going on for ever.

clue.text: Beastly time in the lowest accommodation?

parts.note: a steer is a young bullock, a beast
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A grim stay in the cheapest cabin of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' is not an adjective of dislike here but the beast itself, a STEER.
explanation.definitionFit: On a passenger liner the cheapest berths below decks were the lowest class of passage.

clue.text: Goes under cover when there's gossip in the ship

indicators.note: in the ship places the gossip within the two letters for a steamship

parts.note: SS stands for steamship
to talk is to gossip

explanation.surface: A stowaway hides whenever there is chatter aboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunter who stalks moves stealthily, keeping hidden as he follows his quarry.
